CITATION-NETWORK COMPLIANCE PILOT 01
BOUNDED FOUR-SOURCE POWER-POSING AUDIT
======================================

BOUNDARY NOTICE

This run inspects only S1–S4 in the supplied packet. It does not estimate the
field’s top-50 network, current five-year citation behavior, total internal
density, or field-wide critique uptake. Those questions apply, but the packet
cannot answer them; they are marked PROVISIONAL rather than N/A.

CLAIM MAP MISSING: running in degraded standalone mode. The target claim below
is SELF-GENERATED and PROVISIONAL. Cross-prosecutor claim alignment cannot be
assumed until an upstream Claim Extraction / Inflation Map is produced.

CLAIM MAP: SELF-GENERATED — PROVISIONAL

- Field 1 — What was literally measured:
  S1 randomly assigned 42 participants to high- or low-power poses and measured
  self-reported power, salivary testosterone and cortisol, and one gain-domain
  gambling choice. S2 used a conceptually similar design with 200 participants,
  hormone measures, self-reported power, and three behavioral tasks. S3 reviewed
  33 published experiments on expansive versus contractive posture. S4 applied
  p-curve to the published studies assembled by S3, retaining 24 p-values from
  24 studies after its stated exclusions.

- Field 3 — Weaker defensible claim:
  Expansive postures may increase self-reported feelings of power under some
  laboratory conditions. The four-source packet does not establish reliable
  hormonal or behavioral benefits, field-wide consensus, or practical life
  improvement.

- Field 6 — Claim under audit:
  The cited literature independently establishes that briefly adopting expansive
  power poses produces reliable behavioral and physiological benefits.

PRE-AUDIT CLAIM CONFIRMATION

- Claim under audit (map field 6): The cited literature independently establishes
  reliable behavioral and physiological benefits from brief expansive power poses.
- What was literally measured (map field 1): Small and larger randomized laboratory
  posture manipulations, a narrative review of 33 published experiments, and a
  p-curve analysis of the review’s published-study set.
- Weaker defensible claim (map field 3): Expansive posture may affect self-reported
  feelings of power in some laboratory conditions; broader effects remain contested.
- Target layer: source claim and downstream citation/review synthesis.
- Standalone warning: the Claim Map is SELF-GENERATED — PROVISIONAL, so
  cross-stage alignment remains unresolved.

SECTION A: CITATION NETWORK STRUCTURE AND CARTEL DETECTION

The packet is too small to estimate a top-50 citation network, internal-citation
density, mutual-citation rate, founding-cluster share, or current five-year
behavior. Those questions are applicable and therefore PROVISIONAL, not N/A.

Within the bounded packet, the directed structure is clear:

- S1 is the original focal experiment.
- S2 directly cites S1 and tests a similar claim with an independent author team.
- S3, written by the S1 authors, cites both S1 and S2, summarizes 33 published
  experiments, and proposes potential moderators.
- S4, written by an independent author team, cites S1, S2, and S3 and audits the
  evidential value of the study set assembled by S3.

This is not a mutually supportive four-node closure. Two independent critical
nodes enter the chain, and the failed replication is addressed in the same journal.
The candidate amplification hub is S3 because it gathers 33 published experiments
and reframes the failed replication as a moderator-discovery opportunity. However,
S3 also states that direct replications are needed, which prevents classifying it
as a simple settled-science laundering hub on this packet alone.

Top-50 metrics: PROVISIONAL — no citation database query was performed.
Recent five-year behavior: PROVISIONAL — the packet ends in 2017.
Founding cluster: S1 plus the same-author S3 synthesis, with independent challenge
from S2 and S4.
Field-wide closure: not established.

SECTION B: EVIDENCE TYPE CODING

The four supplied sources contain two primary empirical tests, one narrative
review/commentary, and one methodological critique.

- S1: primary randomized laboratory experiment; direct measurements of hormones,
  self-reported power, and a one-choice risk task.
- S2: primary conceptual replication and extension; direct measurements of the
  same broad outcomes with a larger sample and additional behavioral tasks.
- S3: narrative review/commentary; no new direct test of the focal hormonal and
  behavioral claim, but a table of 33 published experiments with heterogeneous
  outcomes.
- S4: methodological critique using p-curve; direct test of whether the published
  significant-results distribution shows evidential value.

Within the packet, 2 of 4 documents are primary empirical tests, but a document
count is not a measure of evidentiary weight. S1 and S2 directly test the focal
hormonal and behavioral outcomes. S3 aggregates many heterogeneous posture
outcomes and should not be treated as 33 direct replications of the exact S1
claim. S4 tests selective-reporting implications rather than posture effects
directly.

The packet is neither simply evidence-rich nor citation-rich. It contains a real
replication and a real methodological challenge, but it is too bounded to estimate
what proportion of the wider network rests on direct tests, proxies, reviews, or
commentary. Those field-wide percentages are PROVISIONAL.

SECTION C: CITATION POLARITY AND CLAIM USE

Citation relationships were checked by reading the citing and cited sources, so
the classifications below are CROSS-SOURCE-CONFIRMED.

- S2 -> S1: critical/replication-context citation. S2 accurately states S1’s
  reported hormone, risk, and self-report effects, then reports that its larger
  conceptual replication reproduced only self-reported power.
- S3 -> S1: supportive and premise-building. S3 restates S1’s reported outcomes
  as part of a larger published-results review.
- S3 -> S2: critical but substantively engaged. S3 accurately records S2’s null
  hormone and behavior results, identifies procedural differences, proposes
  moderators, and calls for direct replications.
- S4 -> S1: critical background. S4 accurately summarizes the original findings
  and notes their public use.
- S4 -> S2: supportive of the replication challenge. S4 accurately reports that
  S2 found self-reported power but not behavioral or hormonal effects.
- S4 -> S3: critical methodological use. S4 takes S3’s 33-study set as the object
  of p-curve analysis and disputes the inference that the published successes
  establish an effect.

The packet contains serious critical citations inside the same journal and does
not show critique being perfunctorily cited and ignored. Original limitations are
partly preserved: S3 acknowledges the failed replication and explicitly says
direct replications are needed. S4 further narrows the evidentiary claim. The
packet therefore does not support a finding of uniformly supportive citation
polarity.

SECTION D: CLAIM MUTATION TRACKING

The original source already makes a broad causal and practical claim. S1 reports
one randomized laboratory experiment with 42 participants, then states that two
one-minute poses can make a person “instantly become more powerful” and have
real-world actionable implications. The broadening begins at the PAPER layer
rather than requiring later citation mutation.

S3 does not simply convert S1 into settled fact. It accurately states S2’s failed
behavioral and hormonal replication, lists 33 published experiments across
heterogeneous outcomes, proposes potential moderators, and says direct
replications are needed. Its risk is subtler: “33 independent experiments” can
sound like 33 confirmations of one unified power-posing claim even though the
outcomes and paradigms vary. Within this packet that is a moderate synthesis-risk
signal, not verified premise laundering.

S4 does not inflate the claim; it narrows it. It argues that the published study
set does not show evidential value for behavioral and physiological effects after
selective reporting is considered, while allowing that small or future effects
remain possible.

No public or policy source is included. The public/policy step is therefore
PROVISIONAL — not checked — rather than N/A. The bounded academic chain shows
paper-level overreach in S1, a qualified review-level amplification risk in S3,
and corrective narrowing in S4. It does not show monotonic downstream inflation.

SECTION E: ADJACENT FIELD ENGAGEMENT / NEGLECT

Relevant adjacent literatures include replication methodology, publication-bias
analysis, psychophysiology, hormone measurement, demand characteristics, and
measurement theory.

S1 cites hormone, stress, dominance, and embodiment literatures, but the packet
does not establish how thoroughly it engages psychophysiological measurement
risks. S2 uses a larger sample, blinded experimental delivery, and robustness
reasoning. S3 discusses experimenter blindness, demand awareness, social context,
pose duration, and a human-physiology yoga study. S4 brings in publication-bias
and p-curve methodology.

This packet therefore contains visible adjacent-field engagement rather than
obvious categorical neglect. It also shows selective limits: S3 excludes
unpublished findings from its table, which is relevant to publication-bias
analysis, and S4 directly challenges the consequences of that published-only
selection.

The percentage of the dominant field citing adjacent literatures cannot be
estimated from four sources. Canonical-source omission rates and selective-citation
rates are PROVISIONAL. No major adjacent-field-neglect finding is established by
the bounded packet.

SECTION F: HUB DEPENDENCY AND REVIEW-PAPER LAUNDERING

S3 is the candidate hub because it consolidates 33 published experiments and is
the direct target of S4’s p-curve audit. The packet cannot calculate what
percentage of recent papers cite S3, cite S1 directly, or substitute S3 for primary
inspection. Those rates are PROVISIONAL.

S3 preserves several important limits:

- it accurately reports S2’s null behavioral and hormonal results;
- it describes procedural differences rather than pretending the replication
  succeeded;
- it identifies experimenter blindness as a critical variable;
- it says direct replications of S1 and other reports are needed.

S3 also creates amplification risk by presenting 33 published experiments as a
coherent body while excluding unpublished findings and combining heterogeneous
outcomes. S4’s full-text methodological challenge directly contests whether that
published set shows evidential value.

Hub risk within the packet: mild to moderate. S3 is an amplification hub, but the
evidence does not justify “laundering hub” because it preserves the failed
replication and the need for direct tests. Field-wide hub dependency remains
PROVISIONAL.

SECTION G: PATTERN RECOGNITION AND RATCHET BEHAVIOR

The packet shows one potential ratchet pattern but also meaningful model updating.

Potential ratchet: after S2 failed to reproduce S1’s behavioral and hormonal
effects, S3 emphasized procedural differences and possible moderators. Moderator
search can preserve a claim after a failed prediction. Yet S3 did not merely
declare the claim unfalsifiable; it called for direct replications and identified
specific variables that could be tested.

Model updating is visible through S2 and S4. S2 reports a narrower surviving
effect—self-reported power—and rejects the broader behavioral and hormonal result
in its design. S4 treats the broader effects as hypotheses lacking empirical
support. The chain therefore contains correction rather than only premise
expansion.

Intervention escalation, policy ratchets, and outcome-metric substitution are N/A
to this four-paper research packet because no institutional intervention is under
audit. Field-wide reward structure, natural-experiment uptake, and later model
updating are PROVISIONAL because the packet ends in 2017.

SECTION H: IGNORED CRITIQUE AND NON-UPTAKE

The packet contains two serious challenges:

- S2: a larger conceptual replication reporting no hormonal or behavioral effects.
- S4: a p-curve critique of the 33-study published literature assembled by S3.

S2 was not ignored inside the packet. S3 was published alongside it in the same
issue, accurately summarized its results, discussed procedural differences, and
identified future replication needs. That is substantive engagement even if one
disagrees with the moderator framing.

S4 is the last document in the bounded packet. Later uptake, replies, and
rebuttals are outside the fixture. Therefore S4’s subsequent reception is
PROVISIONAL — not checked. The packet cannot support “critique non-uptake” or
suppression. It instead shows critique entering the central journal and shaping
the published exchange.

SECTION I: AUTHOR, INSTITUTION, JOURNAL, AND FUNDING CLUSTERING

Author clustering is present but not closed. S1 and S3 share the same three
authors. S2 is produced by an independent six-author team spanning Zurich,
Stockholm, and Dartmouth. S4 is produced by an independent two-author team.

Journal clustering is complete in the packet: all four items were published in
Psychological Science. That could reflect venue centrality for one controversy,
not gatekeeping. Dissenting work appears in the same venue: S2 and S4 are both
critical and were published by the journal that published S1 and S3.

Institutional clustering is limited. The original/review team and the two critical
teams come from different institutions. Funding overlap is PROVISIONAL because
the packet does not provide a complete, comparable funding record for all four
sources.

Closure type: normal controversy-centered journal clustering with a same-author
review node; insufficient evidence for functional citation closure or explicit
gatekeeping.

SECTION J: FALSE-POSITIVE AND BASELINE CHECK

A four-source controversy packet will naturally be dense because every later item
addresses the same focal claim. Dense citation here is expected and cannot be
benchmarked against a similar subfield without additional data. The comparative
baseline is therefore PROVISIONAL.

Several green flags are present:

- an independent larger replication directly tests the focal outcomes;
- a same-author review acknowledges the failed replication;
- independent critics are published in the same journal;
- S3 states that direct replications are needed;
- S4 publicly specifies its study-selection and p-curve procedure;
- the strong claim is narrowed rather than protected by total non-engagement.

Weaknesses remain:

- S1 makes broad practical claims from a small single study;
- S3’s 33-experiment synthesis aggregates heterogeneous outcomes and excludes
  unpublished findings;
- the packet does not contain a close preregistered direct replication of every
  S1 procedure;
- S4’s later reception is not examined.

The baseline check rejects a cartel label on this packet. It supports a narrower
conclusion: the strong evidentiary claim is contested and not independently
established by the supplied chain.

SECTION J2: THE CONCEDE TEST

| Finding | Concede test: SURVIVES / NARROWS / DEFEATS | Surviving claim if NARROWS |
|---|---|---|
| S1 makes broad actionable claims from one N=42 experiment. | SURVIVES | The wider literature could still independently establish the effects even if S1 overclaimed. |
| S2 reproduces self-reported power but not hormonal or behavioral effects in N=200. | NARROWS | Expansive posture may affect self-reported power in some conditions; reliable hormonal and behavioral benefits are not established by convergence. |
| S3 assembles 33 published experiments across heterogeneous outcomes and excludes unpublished findings. | NARROWS | A published posture literature exists, but its independence and evidential convergence cannot be inferred from the count alone. |
| S4 reports that the eligible published-results p-curve lacks evidential value for downstream behavioral and physiological effects. | DEFEATS | No strong remainder: within this packet, the claim of independent establishment does not follow. |
| Critical work appears in the same journal and S3 substantively engages S2. | SURVIVES | This weakens a closure accusation but does not restore the strong efficacy claim. |
| Top-50 density, current citation behavior, and field-wide uptake were not measured. | SURVIVES | No field-wide network label can be issued; the bounded claim assessment remains possible. |

Scope-loss assessment for NARROWS findings:

| Finding | Scope-loss level | Original claim | Surviving claim | What epistemic or practical work is lost? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S2 larger conceptual replication | MATERIAL NARROWING | Reliable behavioral and physiological benefits are independently established. | Self-reported power may change in some laboratory conditions. | Hormonal, behavioral, and practical recommendations lose support. |
| S3 heterogeneous published-study synthesis | MATERIAL NARROWING | Thirty-three successes demonstrate a coherent effect. | Published studies report varied posture-related outcomes. | The count cannot by itself establish one reliable causal phenomenon or independence from selection. |

The DEFEATS classification applies to the exact epistemic wording in Field 6. It
does not prove that every possible posture effect is false.

SECTION K: CARTEL-RISK SCORING

Scores describe only concern established inside the bounded packet. A zero on an
unmeasured field-wide metric means “no concern established here,” not proof of
absence.

1. Founding-cluster dominance: 1
   Same-author S1/S3 nodes are central, but independent S2/S4 nodes are also
   load-bearing.

2. Internal citation density: 0 — PROVISIONAL field-wide
   The four-node packet is necessarily dense; no top-50 graph was measured.

3. Recent-paper dependence on old cluster: 0 — PROVISIONAL
   The packet contains no 2022–2026 sample.

4. Review-hub laundering: 1
   S3 amplifies a published-success count but preserves the failed replication
   and calls for direct replications.

5. Proxy-to-construct mismatch: 1
   S3 combines heterogeneous posture outcomes that do not all directly test
   reliable hormonal and behavioral benefits.

6. Claim mutation downstream: 1
   The main overreach is already in S1; S3 creates synthesis risk, while S4
   narrows rather than inflates.

7. Adjacent-field neglect: 0 — PROVISIONAL field-wide
   Meta-science and physiology appear in the packet; omission rates were not
   measured.

8. Lack of decisive tests: 2 — FULL-TEXT-CONFIRMED
   S3 explicitly says direct replications are needed; S2 is conceptual rather
   than an exact replication, and S4 disputes the published evidence.

9. Poor critique uptake: 0
   S2 is engaged by S3 in the same issue; S4’s later reception is unmeasured.

10. Intervention ratchet / model non-updating: 0
    No intervention is present, and the packet contains visible claim narrowing.

Total score: 6 / 30.

Numerical interpretation: low-risk within the packet. Formal field-wide label:
insufficient evidence, because the packet was deliberately bounded and cannot
measure the network dimensions required for a healthy-network or cartel verdict.

- Main founding cluster: S1 original experiment plus S3 same-author synthesis.
- Main amplification hub: S3, but only as a candidate bounded-packet hub; field-wide

- Main proxy problem: heterogeneous posture outcomes in S3 cannot all be treated
  as direct confirmations of reliable hormonal and behavioral benefits.
- Main adjacent fields neglected: none established within the packet; field-wide
  engagement rates are PROVISIONAL.
- Main claim mutation: S1 itself moves from one N=42 laboratory experiment to
  instant-power and actionable-life implications; S3 creates qualified synthesis
  amplification; S4 narrows the claim.
- Most important ignored critique: none established. S2 is directly engaged.
  S4’s later reception is PROVISIONAL because the packet ends in 2017.
- Decisive test missing: close, adequately powered, bias-resistant direct
  replications across the specific behavioral and physiological outcomes.
- Cartel-risk score: 6 / 30 within the bounded packet; not a field-wide estimate.
- Load-bearing finding(s): the independent larger replication and S4’s p-curve
  challenge prevent the packet from supporting independent establishment of
  reliable behavioral and physiological benefits.
- Concede-test result: DEFEATS the strong epistemic wording in Field 6; does not

- Failure location: MIXED — PAPER overreach in S1 and CITATION/synthesis risk in S3.

  bounded packet itself is an open, contested citation chain rather than a

  current citation contexts; later replies and replications; direct inspection of

Consistent with the findings of Carney et al., our
results showed a significant effect of power posing on
self-reported feelings of power. However, we found no
significant effect of power posing on hormonal levels or
in any of the three behavioral tasks.

Using a much
larger sample size but similar procedures as Carney et al.
did, we failed to confirm an effect of power posing on
testosterone, cortisol, and financial risk taking. We did
find that power posing affected self-reported feelings of
power; however, this did not yield behavioral effects.

Power Posing: P-Curving the Evidence
Joseph P. Simmons & Uri Simonsohn
University of Pennsylvania

Word Count: 3,202

Forthcoming in Psychological Science

In their response to the failed replication, Carney, Cuddy, and Yap (2015) reviewed 33 successful
studies investigating the effects of expansive vs. contractive posing, focusing on differences between
these studies and the failed replication, to identify possible moderators that future studies could explore.

In this paper we rely on p-curve analysis to answer the following question: Does the literature
reviewed by Carney et al. (2015) suggest the existence of an effect once we account for selective
reporting? We conclude not.

We first evaluated if evidential value was present. As explained in Simonsohn et al. (2015), we
conclude that a literature contains evidential value if either the half p-curve (which only analyzes critical
p-values below .025) is significantly right-skewed at the 5% level, or if both the half and full p-curve are
significantly right skewed at the 10% level. Neither condition is met here (phalf=.11 and pfull=.63,
respectively).
